{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
The phrase "'''hard progeny of the North'''" is a [[misquotation]] from the autobiography (1792) of [[Gilbert Wakefield]]. He wrote that

<blockquote>"It is observed at Cambridge, and is generally true, that the hardy progeny of the North, from [[Cumberland]], [[Westmorland|Westmoreland]], and the remoter parts of [[Yorkshire]], are usually the profoundest proficients in Mathematics and Philosophy."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wakefield |first1=Gilbert |title=Memoirs of the life of ---, B.A. formerly Fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge in two volumes |date=1804 |publisher=J.Johnson |page=83 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ptYB-Don1Q4C&pg=PA83 |language=en}}</ref></blockquote>

An exhibition at [[Lancaster University]] in 1976 took it as title.<ref>Robert Fox and Lois Gray, ''The Hard Progeny of the North. The life and work of eight north country scientists.'' Lancaster, 1976. Library Shelf-mark AK44L</ref>

==Background==
The "hard progeny" were educated in the region's [[Grammar school#Grammar schools in the 18th and 19th centuries|grammar schools]] which were small and typically situated in rural market towns. In an era prior to the dominance of the great public schools, grammar schools were the most important source of entrants to Oxford and Cambridge universities, at least of entrants with serious academic aspirations, especially in north-west England.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Education of the Anglican Clergy, 1780–1839|last=Slinn|first=Sara|publisher=Boydell and Brewer|year=2017|isbn=978-1-78327-175-7|location=Woodbridge|pages=129–169}}</ref>

Richard Watson was described as:<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sT6KLsd94dYC&dq=%22The+Hard+Progeny+Of+The+North%22&pg=PA79|title=The 1702 Chair of Chemistry at Cambridge: Transformation and Change|last1=Archer|first1=Mary D.|last2=Haley|first2=Christopher D.|date=2005-01-06|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780521828734|location=|pages=79|language=en|chapter=3. Richard Watson; gaiters and gunpowder}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=one of 'the hard progeny of the North' who were to enrich British science for a century and more.|sign=|source=The 1702 Chair of Chemistry at Cambridge: Transformation and Change}}

Colin Russell refers to:<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mc7hBwAAQBAJ&dq=%22The+Hard+Progeny+Of+The+North%22&pg=PA16|title=Michael Faraday: Physics and Faith|last=Russell|first=Colin A.|date=2001-01-04|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780190283551|location=|pages=15|language=en}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=These men of science, as well as many others, have been called "the hard progeny of the North," and it seems that the inhospitable climate and the rough terrain must have been one factor in promoting a certain toughness of mind that is so necessary in the pursuit of science.|sign=|source=Michael Faraday: Physics and Faith}}

==The principal individuals==
* [[Richard Watson (bishop of Llandaff)|Richard Watson (1737-1816)]], mathematician; Cambridge professor of chemistry, then theology; Bishop of Llandaff.
* [[Thomas Garnett (physician)|Thomas Garnett (1766-1802)]], physician; professor of natural philosophy at Glasgow, then at the Royal Institution.
* [[John Dawson (surgeon)|John Dawson (1734-1820)]], surgeon, mathematician and notable tutor of mathematics.
* [[Adam Sedgwick|Adam Sedgwick (1784-1873)]], a founder of modern geology; an opponent of evolution.
* [[William_Whewell|William Whewell [1794-1866)]], natural and moral philosopher; philosopher and historian of science.
* [[Richard Owen (geologist)|Richard Owen (1804-1892)]], comparative anatomist, palaeontologist, invented the word "dinosaur".
* [[Edward Frankland|Edward Frankland (1825-1899)]], pioneering professor of chemistry.
* [[William Turner (anatomist)|William Turner (1832-1916)]], professor of anatomy and first English Principal of Edinburgh University.
